ownership_reason: Only the gold sees each element together with the answer of the set (whether set.add took it in); hops 1-3 hold the original list and the set and get the set back, and hop 4 copies the list element for element, clears it and hands the whole copy to the gold, as its javadoc states ('copied, element for element'; 'the copy is then added to the set, element by element in iteration order'). Once the gold has appended a repeated element, no caller can tell from the returned set which list entries are repeats without redoing the gold's work. The gold's javadoc promises that the list keeps the insertion order of the set; on [1, 2, 1] that order is [1, 2] and the variant leaves [1, 2, 1]. The convention is pinned outside the gold: ListOrderedSet.add appends to its order list only on the first addition ('re-adding doesn't change order'; TestListOrderedSet testOrdering re-adds present elements and checks the order), SetUniqueList.add(int, Object) adds to list and set only when the set does not contain the element (TestSetUniqueList testAdd), and SetUniqueList.addAll, the facade's original delegate, ignores duplicates from the added collection (TestSetUniqueList testAddAll); the facade's javadoc states the result ('duplicates ... are removed (first indexed one kept)'). One-line edits above the gold that de-duplicate the copy before the gold (a LinkedHashSet of the list or of the copy at hop 4) pass the existing tests but contradict hop 4's documented element-for-element copy and hand-over and re-implement the gold's decision; a HashSet copy at hop 4 passes only because Integer 1 and 2 hash in that order and reorders other lists.
